chapters.title: Find Someone Who's Solved Your Problem
chapters.hook: A competitor's cart rolls past the endcap and turns into a new option.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the romance of originality, better options often begin with a borrowed pattern. The work is to translate the pattern, not copy the costume.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When options feel thin, search for solved versions of the same pattern: outside peers, internal bright spots, playlists, and distant analogies give you raw material to adapt.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next stuck-choice conversation, write 'Who has solved this pattern already?' Read it aloud, then note the first source named.

breakdown.fastRead:
Sam Walton turns a store aisle into a notebook. A competitor's display, checkout flow, or shelf sign is not an enemy secret. It is a worked example. He studies the pattern, then asks what Walmart could adapt. Borrow patterns, not costumes.

Call the move analogical search: look outside the tight choice for a solved version of the same problem. Search peers, nearby bright spots, prompt lists, and distant fields. Do not copy. Widen the options when ideas run dry.
breakdown.deepRead:
A stuck choice often feels like a blank page because the team keeps staring at its own table. Analogical search changes the room. It asks, who has already wrestled with this pattern, even if their name for it differs?

A retailer, a nurse, and a designer all begin with the same small act. They name the constraint in plain words. A store needs a better way to move shoppers. A hospital needs sepsis care that works more often. A swimsuit designer needs speed through water. Then the search widens by degrees. Look at direct peers. Look nearby for places already doing better. Use a playlist, which is a short set of search prompts. A playlist opens search; a checklist protects steps.

Kaiser Permanente's sepsis work shows why the best clue may be nearby. Some care units are already getting better results under the same roof, with the same broad rules and pressures. Those internal bright spots prove that success is not fantasy. Bright spots make hope local. The useful question becomes, what are they doing that others can study?

Harriet's copied endcap shows the trap. A copied best practice can go stale fast, especially once everyone has it. A borrowed pattern still has to fit the local facts. Sam Walton did not need every rival's store to become Walmart. He needed each store to teach him one option he had not seen alone.
breakdown.fullRead:
Fiona Fairhurst did not have to stay inside swimwear to think about swimwear. Speedo's Fastskin design looked toward fast movement through water, including sharkskin-like inspiration. That move is called laddering up. You climb from the narrow object to the broader job it must do.

Laddering up helps when the closest comparison is too cramped. If the search stays with other swimsuit makers, it stays inside familiar fabric and seams. If the search moves to what travels quickly through water, it gets wider. Biology, boats, and other sports can enter the room.

Here analogy can become silly. A shark is not a swimsuit factory. Nature is not handing over a pattern sheet. The useful step is to ask what principle is portable. In Fastskin's case, the shared pattern is movement through water. The designer still has to turn that pattern into material, fit, and rules for swimmers.

Use the same care with benchmarking. Sam Walton's habit of studying competitors is powerful because it treats the world as a live library. Yet a rival's best practice may stop helping once every rival has copied it. It may also work only because of that rival's staff, customers, or cost structure. Search has to keep moving after the first good-looking answer.

Playlists help here because they keep the search active. A checklist says, do not miss these steps. A playlist asks, where else might an option come from? Try outside peers. Try internal bright spots. Try a different field that shares the same constraint. Try a broader category than the one named on the problem.

A borrowed answer also needs a fit check before it enters the plan. Write the admired practice in two columns: the job it performs and the conditions that let it work. If either column stays blank, the team has found an interesting story, not yet a usable option.

The move breaks down when the underlying problem is not the same. A hospital unit with a sepsis bright spot may teach care habits to another Kaiser unit. It cannot settle a staffing dispute, replace clinical judgment, or prove a treatment works without evidence. Copying the visible behavior without the working mechanism turns analogy into theater.

So name the pattern before borrowing the solution. Ask what job the admired practice performs, what local constraint it survived, and what would have to change here. When the match is real, someone else's solved problem becomes a new path. When the match is shallow, the borrowed answer is only a costume with better lighting.

examples.title: Aisle Thread
examples.scenario:
During a Monday store-opening walk at Walmart, floor manager Cameron sends Sandrine a photo of a rival checkout lane.
Cameron: Sam Walton would have asked why that line moves faster.
Sandrine: Copy the layout?
Cameron: Not yet. First name what problem it solved.
Sandrine: The line bends away from the entrance.
Cameron: Then our option is not their lane. It is a better way to keep waiting shoppers from blocking new ones.
examples.whatToDo: Cameron writes the rival's practice as a problem-solution pair before he suggests a change. He turns the competitor into a prompt, not a template.
examples.whyItMatters: Benchmarking helps when it widens the option set. It fails when the team copies the surface and misses the constraint the practice solved.

examples.title: Sepsis Pause
examples.scenario: Asha begins the Kaiser Permanente huddle with an outside consultant's sepsis slide in her hand. Then she stops, sets the slide facedown, and restarts with the unit list. Two Kaiser teams are already catching sepsis sooner under the same rules. The new first move is to call those nurses and ask what sequence they trust before the warning signs scatter.
examples.whatToDo: Asha resets the search toward internal bright spots. She asks the better-performing units for the repeatable habits behind their sepsis results.
examples.whyItMatters: A bright spot inside the same system has already survived local limits. That makes it a strong source of options before the team imports a foreign fix.

examples.title: Tank Ripple
examples.scenario: Travis watches a strip of Fastskin test fabric ripple in the Speedo tank. A note beside it names Fiona Fairhurst and sharkskin, but the cloth is not pretending to be an animal. Tiny changes in the surface catch the water differently. The live question on the bench is wider than swimwear: what forms move through water with less drag?
examples.whatToDo: Travis ladders up from swimsuit to speed through water. He treats sharkskin-style inspiration as a design clue that still has to become fabric.
examples.whyItMatters: Distant analogies work when they transfer a principle. They mislead when the team tries to copy nature as if it were a finished product.

examples.title: Playlist Talk
examples.scenario:
During a store operations call, regional manager Helene taps a pen beside the shelf-flow agenda. "So the Sam Walton move is a checklist?"
"No," Harriet says. "A checklist keeps us from missing a step. This is a playlist. Which competitor, which internal store, which other field?"
Helene circles candidates on the agenda. "So we are not obeying the list. We are using it to find options."
examples.whatToDo: Helene rewrites the meeting note from tasks to search prompts. She uses the playlist to name option sources before judging any one answer.
examples.whyItMatters: A checklist protects execution after a choice. A playlist helps before the choice, when the team needs more places to look.

examples.title: Best Practice Slip
examples.scenario: At the Friday Walmart merchandising review, category lead Harriet is halfway through praising a rival's endcap when her marker freezes above the board. She has skipped the fit check. Every competitor has seen the same display, and her store's shoppers enter from a different side. She crosses out copy it and writes test the job: slow the rush, lift the item, fit our entrance.
examples.whatToDo: Harriet catches her own copying mistake and reframes the practice around the job it performs. She keeps the search open after the first attractive example.
examples.whyItMatters: Best practices can lose value when everyone copies them or when the context changes. Adapt the working mechanism before the practice becomes local policy.

examples.title: Analogy Memo
examples.scenario: At a Tuesday Speedo design review, product lead Elijah hands the team a one-page memo. It reads: "Do not stop at other suits. Fiona Fairhurst's Fastskin work points us up one rung, from swimwear to fast movement through water. Search sharkskin-style surfaces, hulls, and racing gear. Bring back principles, not shapes. A close competitor may share our category while missing our deeper constraint."
examples.whatToDo: Elijah uses the memo to widen the analogy search before the team picks a direction. He names the broader category and the rule for translating it.
examples.whyItMatters: Laddering up prevents the team from treating the nearest rival as the only teacher. The best analogy may share the job, not the industry.

questions.prompt: You are stuck on a store-layout choice, and your own team has no fresh ideas. Which next search fits solved-problem thinking?
choices: Study solved layout problems and adapt the pattern they used.
Delay the search until the team protects originality with an inside idea.
Pick the familiar layout so the store avoids borrowing outside practice.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports finding solved versions of a similar problem. The other choices treat borrowing as a threat, which is the common error.

questions.prompt: A manager studies Sam Walton's habit of watching competitors. What should she take from the Walmart case?
choices: Competitor visits matter when the rival's practice can be copied without changes.
Competitor visits can reveal working practices that become raw material for options.
Competitor visits mainly prove which retailer already owns the best answer.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says Walton used external observation to generate options. Exact copying is the misconception this search method rejects.

questions.prompt: At Kaiser Permanente, a sepsis team finds two units already doing better. Why should those units matter?
choices: They can replace broader evidence because local results share many constraints.
They can prove the problem is solved before anyone studies the practice.
They can reveal a workable pattern under constraints the system shares.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 makes internal bright spots useful because they succeed under similar constraints. They do not end the work or replace evidence.

questions.prompt: A hospital leader calls Kaiser sepsis bright spots mere anecdotes. Which reply best fits the source fact?
choices: They help mainly when a positive story raises morale across units.
They matter only after an outside expert names them best practice.
They help when teams study better results for repeatable mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says internal performance differences become valuable when studied for repeatable patterns. Treating them as morale stories is too thin.

questions.prompt: You draft a short list of prompts: peers, internal bright spots, and distant fields. What kind of tool is that list?
choices: It is a playlist that helps generate options when the page feels blank.
It is a checklist that prevents missed steps after the plan is chosen.
It is a rulebook that decides which option the team must choose.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 defines playlists as prompt sets for option generation. Checklists protect execution, and rulebooks decide more than this tool can.

questions.prompt: A designer uses a sports analogy only after the product choice is done, as a way to sell the decision. What did she miss?
choices: Analogies should stay close to the home industry so teams trust them.
Analogies work best as proof that the chosen answer was obvious later.
Analogies should guide option search before the team settles on an answer.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 treats analogies as search tools before the decision. Using them only as later decoration misses the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A Speedo Fastskin discussion turns sharkskin into a literal copy target. What correction fits the case?
choices: Use the shared water-speed pattern and adapt the principle into design.
Use the organism as a blueprint because nature finished the design work.
Use only other swimsuits because biology sits outside the product category.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 supports adapting the water-movement principle. It rejects both literal copying and staying only with direct competitors.

questions.prompt: A team finds a famous best practice and wants to stop searching. What warning should slow them down?
choices: A best practice is useful only before competitors notice and copy it.
A copied practice can lose fit or freshness, so adaptation still matters.
A famous practice should be rejected because borrowing weakens original thinking.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 warns that copied best practices can stop differentiating or fit poorly. The answer is adaptation, not automatic rejection.

questions.prompt: A product team keeps comparing itself with the closest rival and finds nothing new. What should laddering up change?
choices: It should narrow the search to the rival customers compare most often.
It should shift from the product to a broader category with the same constraint.
It should pause all comparisons until the team has finished a prototype.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says laddering up broadens the search from the specific case to a wider category. The closest competitor may not be the best analogy.

reviewCards.front: What does analogical search ask you to do before judging the first option?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to look for solved versions of the same pattern, then adapt what worked. The search may run through competitors, peers, internal bright spots, playlists, or distant fields.

reviewCards.front: What are the four moves in solved-problem search?
reviewCards.back: Use all four: Benchmark outside, Find internal bright spots, Use playlists, and Ladder up through analogies. Together they keep the option search from staying too local.

reviewCards.front: Why can an internal bright spot beat a glamorous outside example?
reviewCards.back: A local success has already worked under similar constraints. Kaiser Permanente's sepsis bright spots matter because they show a pattern that survived inside the same system.

reviewCards.front: How is a playlist different from a checklist during option search?
reviewCards.back: A playlist opens the search before a choice by asking where options might come from. A checklist protects execution after a choice by guarding against missed steps.

reviewCards.front: Where does Four decision villains (Ch 1) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: The villains help you see that a narrow frame may be starving the option set. They mislead if you only name the bias and never go find peers, bright spots, playlists, or analogies.

reviewCards.front: Why does laddering up help when the nearest competitor teaches nothing new?
reviewCards.back: Laddering up moves from the product to the broader job it performs. Speedo Fastskin could look beyond suits because the deeper category was fast movement through water.

implementationPlan.title: Ask the Solver Question
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a stuck choice into a search for solved patterns. Ask the Solver Question means you name the problem in plain words, then ask who has already solved that kind of problem. The skill is translation: bring back the mechanism, not the costume.

ifThenPlans.context: If a competitor's practice looks tempting
ifThenPlans.plan: If the rival's move looks useful, then Ask the Solver Question by writing the problem it solved before copying any surface detail.

ifThenPlans.context: If an outside expert seems like the only source
ifThenPlans.plan: If the team reaches outside first, then Ask the Solver Question inside the system by naming one bright spot already working under similar constraints.

ifThenPlans.context: If the room goes blank during option generation
ifThenPlans.plan: If nobody has a candidate, then Ask the Solver Question from a playlist: peer, internal bright spot, distant field, broader category.

ifThenPlans.context: If the closest comparison keeps giving stale answers
ifThenPlans.plan: If the direct rival teaches nothing new, then Ask the Solver Question one rung up by naming the broader job the choice must do.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During the next conversation about a stuck choice today, write one sentence: 'This problem is like ___ because ___.' Read it aloud and record the source it points to.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of the week, review one choice where you used Ask the Solver Question. Name what changed about your search: the source, the pattern, or the option you adapted.

memorableLines.text: Borrow patterns, not costumes.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the borrowing warning into one portable line.

memorableLines.text: A playlist opens search; a checklist protects steps.
memorableLines.why: It separates two tools readers often confuse.

memorableLines.text: Bright spots make hope local.
memorableLines.why: It makes the Kaiser Permanente lesson easy to recall.

chapters.title: Consider the Opposite
chapters.hook: If 2 of 10 deal facts flatter the buyer, what hides in the other 8?
chapters.counterintuition: A skeptical voice can sound like delay. In fact, the fastest safe path is often the one that lets a loved option lose early.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next coffee or commute, say to one person, "Tell me one clue I am missing." Listen, then write their exact phrase before you answer.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before defending a favored choice, ask what would have to be true for another answer to win, then look for the facts that could beat you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Mathew Hayward and Donald Hambrick studied deals where confident CEOs paid acquisition premiums. One public summary puts the average premium at 41%. The buyer sees praise, recent wins, and a target that looks like proof. The missing facts sit outside the warm circle of yes. A favored answer needs a fair enemy.

Considering the opposite means inviting evidence that could make your first answer lose. Ask which facts would let a rival option win. Then seek the person, number, or test that could prove it. Doubt earns trust when it can change the call.
breakdown.deepRead:
Praise changes the search. When a leader has been winning, the mind starts looking for facts that fit the story. Confirmation bias is that tilt toward friendly proof. It shapes the question before the answer appears. Joanne may ask, "Will this deal help us grow?" and hear a room full of ways it might. She gets a different room if she asks, "What fact would make us walk away?"

Roger Martin's question helps because it lowers the heat. Nobody has to say, "Your plan is bad." Lola points at Option A: "For this to be best, churn has to fall fast." For Option B, sales costs must stay low. The group is no longer voting on egos. It is hunting for conditions.

A murder board does the same work with sharper lights. Gloria brings a proposal before people told to test it hard. A devil's advocate role can help, but only if the critic names evidence. A loud objection is cheap. A testable objection is useful. The room should leave with a list of assumptions that would change the choice if they failed.

Questions make the bias visible. Ask a vendor, "This will integrate cleanly, right?" and the answer will likely smile back. Ask, "Which client had the hardest integration, and what broke first?" and the answer has to carry weight. Friendly questions feed friendly stories.

The opposite is not a mood. It is a search plan.
breakdown.fullRead:
Nathan has 20 minutes before the acquisition review ends, and the slide with the 41% premium is still on the screen. He likes the deal. The target fills a gap his team has talked about for months. Praise for the CEO is in the background too, the kind Hayward and Hambrick treated as part of hubris risk. Nathan can feel the room leaning toward yes.

He asks for one more pass. Not a debate about whether people are brave or weak. Just a table with three columns: what must be true, how we would know, and who will check. The room slows down. A sales lead names renewal rates. A finance lead asks how much of the premium depends on fast cost cuts. A quiet analyst asks whether recent strong results are making everyone overread the fit.

That is where the method earns its keep. It gives dissent a job. The dissenter is not there to sneer at hope. She is there to make hope prove itself. Roger Martin's wording keeps the work clean: if this option were best, what would have to be true? The answer may still favor the deal. If it does, the team can say yes with fewer blind spots.

The same habit fits smaller calls. Theodore is hiring for a role and likes the first candidate. Instead of asking each reference, "Was she great?" he asks for a hard example. "Where did she need the most coaching?" The reference pauses. The pause is useful. It means the question reached a place praise would have skipped.

Murder boards carry the hard edge. A devil's advocate who performs doubt for 5 minutes and then folds has not helped. Spencer needs the board to name the test that could kill his proposal. If the risk is integration, ask for the last failed integration. If the risk is overpaying, ask what result would make the premium look foolish. If the risk is false confidence, ask who benefits if everyone keeps nodding.

Controlled mistakes can also test stale beliefs. Sylvain's team assumes a review step catches every weak claim. For one low-risk proposal, he plants a known weak claim and watches whether the process catches it. The miss is not a stunt. It is evidence. A small planned flaw can reveal a large hidden faith.

This practice costs comfort. Joanne has to let a colleague poke the line she wants to defend. Lola has to write down the fact that would make her preferred option lose. Gloria has to hear that her careful proposal still rests on guesses. The price is pride paid in advance, before the market charges interest.

Do not turn this into ritual doubt. Some teams appoint a critic, nod through the pushback, and keep the same decision. That is theater. The test is simple: did anyone name evidence that could change the answer? If not, the room protected the favorite. If yes, the favorite has started to earn its place.

The cost is giving up the warm speed of agreement. The gain is a choice that has survived a real opponent.

examples.title: Premium on Trial
examples.scenario: Joanne closes the acquisition packet in an executive deal review after Nathan praises the target again. The 41% average premium from Mathew Hayward and Donald Hambrick's hubris work sits on the finance slide. Nathan says the CEO's strong year proves the company can absorb the price. Joanne answers, "Confidence is not evidence until it survives a hostile fact."
examples.whatToDo: Joanne asks Nathan to name one fact that would make the premium too high, then assigns a finance lead to find that fact before the vote.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe makes dissent part of the deal process. It protects the group from treating praise, recent wins, and status as proof of value.

examples.title: Strategy Class Conditions
examples.scenario: Lola is tutoring a night strategy class when Theodore pushes two option sheets across the table. He keeps asking which option Roger Martin would pick. Lola writes, "what would have to be true," above both columns on the whiteboard. Theodore frowns, then lists churn, price, and sales cost as facts each option needs.
examples.whatToDo: Lola keeps Theodore from voting too soon. She makes him write the conditions that would let either option win, then choose which conditions need proof.
examples.whyItMatters: The class scene shows why the wording works. It moves learners from defending a side to checking the facts each side depends on.

examples.title: Board Before Launch
examples.scenario: Gloria once ran proposal reviews from a call center pod with a devil's advocate who gave one sharp speech and then went quiet. The launch still failed on a basic demand claim. Months later, she opens a murder board with the same binder and a new rule: every attack must name the evidence that would change the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Gloria changes the board from performance to proof. She accepts objections only when they point to a test, a missing number, or a customer fact.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast makes the hard edge plain. A critic role helps only when it creates evidence the team must face before reality does.

examples.title: Reference Check Turn
examples.scenario: Nathan takes a returned phone call from a reference while Spencer waits beside the hiring rubric. "Ask if she was great," Nathan says. Spencer shakes his head. "Roger Martin would call that assumption testing. Ask where she needed coaching." Nathan repeats the question into the phone. The pause tells them more than another polished yes would have.
examples.whatToDo: Spencer pushes Nathan from a confirmatory question to a probing one. The call asks for a hard example, not a warm summary.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows how bias hides inside question wording. A better question makes room for specifics that praise would smooth over.

examples.title: The Deal in Theodore's Head
examples.scenario: Theodore drafts an investment memo at an analyst workbench while the deal model recalculates. No one speaks. He searches for "acquisition premium justified" and likes the first chart. Then Mathew Hayward and Donald Hambrick's 41% premium anchor nags at him. Wrong search, he thinks. Try "CEO hubris overpay failed acquisition" before the memo chooses for me.
examples.whatToDo: Theodore rewrites his search terms to find contrary evidence first. He adds a note naming the result that would make him cut the premium.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene puts confirmation bias inside one mind. The fix begins before debate, with the words used to search for evidence.

examples.title: Scarce Hour for Doubt
examples.scenario: Sylvain stands beside the planning-room wall before the annual agenda locks, sketching time blocks on an index card. The team has one spare hour. He can give it to slide polish, or he can run a murder board with a devil's advocate who must name two assumptions and one deliberate mistake that would test them.
examples.whatToDo: Sylvain gives the scarce hour to the murder board. He defines the critic's job as finding evidence tests, not making a dramatic speech.
examples.whyItMatters: The planning choice shows the price of real skepticism. Time spent testing assumptions cannot also be spent making the favorite look smoother.

questions.prompt: Your product team prefers a new feature and keeps searching for comments that praise it. Which concern best fits confirmation bias?
choices: The team may need a larger sample before the praise can guide the launch choice.
The team may be shaping search terms and interpretation around the answer it wants.
The team may be moving too slowly because praise has already made the launch clear.
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias tilts search and reading toward the preferred answer. A bigger sample helps only if the team also seeks evidence that could disconfirm the feature.

questions.prompt: A board sees a beloved CEO propose an acquisition after a strong year. Which warning should stay on the table?
choices: The premium may be required by the market because most targets demand a high price.
The premium may reflect overconfidence fed by praise, recent wins, and self-importance.
The premium may be safer if the CEO presents more success stories from the same year.
questions.explanation: Hayward and Hambrick link hubris with acquisition premiums. The warning is not that every premium is irrational, but that confidence can inflate the price.

questions.prompt: An analyst points to a 41% premium and says the target must be worth it because the buyer agreed to pay. What is the best reply?
choices: The premium may show that the buyer has rare insight into value others have missed.
The premium may show that the target has drawn enough interest to justify speed.
The premium raises the hurdle and may reflect optimism or overconfidence, not proof of value.
questions.explanation: The 41% premium is a danger signal because it makes value harder to create. Payment size alone does not prove the target is worth the price.

questions.prompt: When Gloria invites dissent before a launch, which version is most likely to fight hubris rather than just slow the meeting?
choices: She asks each critic to bring one piece of contrary evidence that could change the launch plan.
She lets every critic state a concern, then returns to the plan once everyone feels heard.
She asks critics to wait until after launch so the team can move with more energy.
questions.explanation: Constructive disagreement helps when dissent brings information the favorite plan suppresses. A concern with no evidence can become ceremony.

questions.prompt: In a strategy session, Roger Martin's question would steer a tense group toward which task?
choices: Name the conditions that would make each option the best choice.
Ask each side to admit which person in the room has the weaker case.
Rank the speakers by confidence before checking the facts behind them.
questions.explanation: The question asks what would have to be true. It tests conditions and evidence, which lowers blame and keeps people from attacking one another.

questions.prompt: A hiring manager likes a candidate and asks, "She was excellent, right?" Which replacement question better tests the choice?
choices: Would your team hire her again if the same role opened next quarter?
Can you describe the project where she looked strongest to senior leaders?
Where did she need coaching, and what pattern showed up more than once?
questions.explanation: A probing question asks for specifics and possible weakness. The other questions can still invite praise for a candidate the manager already likes.

questions.prompt: A team names Spencer as devil's advocate, lets him object for 5 minutes, and changes nothing. What went wrong?
choices: Spencer should have been given a warmer title so the team would hear him as helpful.
Spencer should have objected after the decision so the team could stay focused first.
Spencer needed evidence standards and assumptions whose failure would change the choice.
questions.explanation: A devil's advocate role works only when it creates real tests. Without assumptions and evidence standards, the role becomes theater.

questions.prompt: Your review process claims it catches weak assumptions. Which small test best matches the deliberate-mistake idea?
choices: Skip the review once and see whether the team finishes the work faster.
Plant one low-risk weak claim and see whether the process catches it.
Ask reviewers whether the process feels strict enough before the next proposal.
questions.explanation: A controlled mistake creates evidence about the process. It is safer than trusting an inherited belief that the review works.

questions.prompt: During WRAP's reality-testing phase, Nathan gathers 30 pages supporting the option he already favors. What should change?
choices: He should seek disconfirming evidence, since more friendly data can deepen the bias.
He should gather another 30 pages, since volume is the main cure for weak reality testing.
He should move back to option generation, since reality testing is mostly about widening.
questions.explanation: Reality testing fights confirmation bias. More data is not enough if all of it supports the preferred answer.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean to consider the opposite before a decision hardens?
reviewCards.back: It means naming the evidence that could make your favored option lose, then seeking that evidence before commitment. The goal is not gloom; it is a fair test.

reviewCards.front: How does Roger Martin's question make disagreement less personal?
reviewCards.back: It asks what would have to be true for an option to win. People can test conditions, numbers, and facts instead of proving another person wrong.

reviewCards.front: Why can CEO praise and recent success make an acquisition premium riskier?
reviewCards.back: Praise and strong results can feed hubris. The buyer may treat confidence as proof, pay a higher premium, and ignore facts that would make the deal less attractive.

reviewCards.front: When does a devil's advocate become theater instead of help?
reviewCards.back: It becomes theater when the critic merely objects and the team keeps the same plan. The role helps only when it names assumptions and tests that could change the answer.

reviewCards.front: Why are probing questions stronger than confirmatory questions?
reviewCards.back: Probing questions ask for specifics, hard cases, and counterevidence. Confirmatory questions invite the answer you want and can make confidence look like proof.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how does Narrow frame (Ch 2) connect to considering the opposite?
reviewCards.back: A narrow frame hides other options; considering the opposite tests the chosen option by asking what facts could make another path win.

implementationPlan.title: Ask the Losing Fact
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice asking for the fact that could make your favorite answer lose. Use a simple order: name the preferred option, name the rival condition, then ask one person for the evidence you are missing. The skill is not arguing longer. It is making disproof safe enough to enter the room.

ifThenPlans.context: If your search results mostly flatter the answer you already like
ifThenPlans.plan: If the evidence feels too friendly, then rewrite the search around the failure case and read the strongest contrary result first.

ifThenPlans.context: If a group starts defending people instead of testing options
ifThenPlans.plan: If the room gets personal, then ask what would have to be true for each option to be best.

ifThenPlans.context: If an expert gives a confident answer that supports your plan
ifThenPlans.plan: If the answer arrives too smoothly, then ask for a specific case where the plan failed or needed repair.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone is named devil's advocate
ifThenPlans.plan: If the role sounds symbolic, then require two assumptions and one evidence test before the meeting ends.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the next choice you defend today, say one sentence aloud: "The fact that could beat me is _____." Fill the blank, then ask one person where to look for that fact.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time you ask for disconfirming evidence before a decision. At week's end, read the number and choose one setting where the count should rise.

memorableLines.text: A favored answer needs a fair enemy.
memorableLines.why: It makes dissent feel like a test of the choice, not an attack on the chooser.

memorableLines.text: The opposite is not a mood.
memorableLines.why: It warns readers that real skepticism needs a search plan, not a pose.

memorableLines.text: A loud objection is cheap.
memorableLines.why: It separates noisy criticism from evidence that can change a decision.

chapters.title: Zoom Out, Zoom In
chapters.hook: You trust the vivid plan; what if the old failure rate is the clue you need?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does a forecast feel stronger after you add detail, even when the detail hides the odds? A good choice uses the average first, then walks close enough to see what the average leaves out.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you open a decision file, move the forecast page beside the closest past-case note until you add one base rate and one lived-detail note.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Reality testing improves when you zoom out for base rates, zoom in for lived detail, and refuse to let either numbers or stories decide alone.

breakdown.fastRead:
Jack's Thai restaurant plan feels vivid: menu ideas, a room full of guests, and a founder who can see why this place will beat the odds. The missing item is less vivid but more useful: what happens to similar restaurants? Base rates cool the story before the story runs the room.

Zooming out means asking for the record from comparable cases. Zooming in means getting close to the lived facts. Use both. The average keeps hope from making a private forecast too rosy. The close-up keeps the average from hiding Monday's lived cost.
breakdown.deepRead:
A forecast gets safer when it moves between two distances. From far away, similar cases show the rough odds. From close up, people and small details show what the choice will ask of daily life. Either lens alone can mislead.

Daniel Kahneman's curriculum team had an inside story that made sense. They knew the work, the talent in the room, and the steps on the plan. Then comparable projects pointed to a much longer timeline. The outside view was not smarter because it knew the people better. It was smarter because it had seen more cases.

Ask experts for the kind of answer they are best placed to give. A seasoned operator may be weak at naming your one true future, but strong at naming a reference class. How long do projects like this usually take? How often do restaurants like Jack's make it? What happens when teams with similar plans hit the same wall?

Close-up stories warm the average without letting it drive alone. Brian Zikmund-Fisher did not need only medical odds before transplant treatment. He needed to hear what patients lived through: the fatigue, the fear, the dull practical parts of recovery. The odds mattered. The lived detail mattered too. The skill is not picking numbers over stories. The skill is making each lens do its own job.
breakdown.fullRead:
Brian Zikmund-Fisher's transplant choice shows why averages can be too thin. A survival number can guide risk, but it cannot tell someone what the hallway smells like after treatment, how tired a patient feels, or which small daily tasks become hard. For a choice someone must live, that kind of detail belongs in the room.

The danger is letting a close-up story become the whole case. One patient account can be honest and still not typical. One restaurant owner can be skilled and still face the failure rate of restaurants. One project team can be bright and still run into the same delay pattern that caught other teams. Numbers anchor the forecast; stories test the landing.

Outside view means looking for a reference class: a group of similar cases. Jack's Thai restaurant belongs to a wider class of new restaurants. Kahneman's curriculum project belonged to a wider class of curriculum projects. A hiring plan, house remodel, software build, or treatment choice has a wider class too. The class will not match perfectly. It does not have to. It gives the first estimate before pride edits the forecast.

Inside view means looking at the case from its own details. That view is not a villain. It catches facts the average cannot see: a chef's skill, a team's budget, a patient's support at home, a vendor's known weakness. Trouble starts when those details feel so special that the reference class disappears. The inside story starts saying, not us.

A useful sequence is plain. First zoom out. Ask what happened to similar cases and what base rate should be the starting point. Next zoom in. Ask what lived details should adjust the start. Then keep the adjustment modest unless the local evidence is strong. A forecast that starts with the average and then moves for real differences is less likely to be captured by hope.

Experts fit the same rule. Do not ask only, will this exact thing work? Ask what class the expert would put it in, what outcomes are common there, and what features usually move the odds. A doctor, builder, founder, or teacher may have seen dozens of cases. Their memory of the class can be more useful than their confidence about your one case.

This is also a kindness to the people who will live with the decision. Averages can make a choice look clean from a distance. Close-up accounts make the afterlife of the choice visible. A bone marrow transplant is not only a probability. A restaurant is not only a failure rate. A project is not only a date on a plan. The person deciding needs both the cold estimate and the warm texture.

When should you do the opposite? If you already have a solid base rate and the next story is only a bid to make the favorite option feel special, stop collecting stories. Zooming in should add lived detail, not excuse the forecast from the evidence. When the story starts asking to overrule the whole class, go back to the class.

examples.title: Jack's Menu Talk
examples.scenario: Helena asks, "What makes Jack's Thai restaurant different?" Phyllis names the chef, the menu, and the block near the train stop. Helena taps the lease draft on her desk and asks for one more number before they bless the forecast: the failure rate for restaurants like this one. Phyllis pauses. The plan still sounds good, but the room has a new fact to find.
examples.whatToDo: Helena keeps the menu story in view, then asks Phyllis to bring the restaurant base rate before they treat Jack's forecast as special.
examples.whyItMatters: The dialogue shows the inside view doing useful work without ruling alone. A vivid plan earns a hearing, but the reference class gets a vote.

examples.title: The Curriculum Gap
examples.scenario: At a Wednesday curriculum workshop, Grace copies milestones onto a whiteboard for a team of education planners and expects the Daniel Kahneman case to end with a neat planning win. The experts know the work, so the estimate should be sharp. Then the outside-view record arrives: similar curriculum projects took much longer. The surprise is that skill did not save the insider forecast.
examples.whatToDo: Grace keeps the team's milestone plan, then resets the forecast from comparable curriculum projects before adding any local adjustment.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal teaches why base rates can beat detailed plans. Expertise helps most when it finds the right comparison group, not when it crowns the plan.

examples.title: Patient Voices Thread
examples.scenario: Justine texts Cyrielle: "The bone marrow transplant odds are in the packet." Cyrielle replies, "Good. What did Brian Zikmund-Fisher seek next?" Justine sends three patient notes: fatigue after visits, fear before counts, help needed at home. Cyrielle answers, "Now the number has a life around it." The decision is still open, but it is less flat.
examples.whatToDo: Justine keeps the medical odds on the table and adds patient experiences so the transplant choice includes practical burdens.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows zooming in as a complement, not a revolt against data. Lived detail tells the reader what the average cannot show.

examples.title: Expert Question Reset
examples.scenario: On a Monday contractor call from the front hall, Ethan starts as a homeowner asking, "Will our remodel finish before school starts?" The old routine wants a yes or no. He pauses with the pen still uncapped. Then he restarts: "For homes like ours, how often does the job run past the first date, and what usually causes it?" The expert shifts from one bright promise to a base-rate answer.
examples.whatToDo: Ethan changes the expert question from a single prediction to a reference-class estimate, then asks what local facts should move the estimate.
examples.whyItMatters: Experts are often strongest when they describe many cases they have seen. The reset makes their experience useful without asking for a magic forecast.

examples.title: Lease Packet Detail
examples.scenario: Curtis stands in the retail stockroom with a lease packet, a takeout menu, and a foot-traffic count clipped together. The Thai restaurant failure rate sits in blue ink at the top. Under it are smaller notes: lunch rush, nearby offices, delivery access, rent due date. No one has decided yet. The page simply refuses to let one kind of evidence crowd out the other.
examples.whatToDo: Curtis puts the base rate at the top of the packet and adds site details underneath, so the lease forecast begins with the class and then adjusts.
examples.whyItMatters: The vignette makes the two-lens habit visible. A forecast gets steadier when the average and the local facts share the same page.

examples.title: Anecdote Course Correction
examples.scenario: Phyllis reads one transplant patient's account in the clinic waiting area and feels her whole choice tilt toward that story. Then she hears herself say, "So this is what will happen." She catches the error mid-sentence. Brian Zikmund-Fisher looked for patient experience to fill in the odds, not to replace them. Phyllis marks the story as texture, then returns to the broader numbers.
examples.whatToDo: Phyllis labels the patient story as lived detail and checks it beside the transplant base rates before letting it change the decision.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery protects the hard edge. Zooming in adds the feel of a choice, but it should not let one account overrule the evidence.

questions.prompt: You are drawn to Jack's detailed restaurant plan because the menu, staff, and location feel vivid. What should you remember about the inside view?
choices: It can reveal useful local detail, but it can also underweight outcomes from similar restaurants.
It should be dropped once any restaurant base rate appears in the discussion.
It gives the safest forecast when the plan has enough concrete detail.
questions.explanation: The inside view is not useless. It carries detail, but vivid detail can make the case feel too unique and push comparable outcomes out of sight.

questions.prompt: A project team has a polished schedule and asks how to reality-test the date. Which first estimate best uses the outside view?
choices: Ask the most confident planner to give a single final completion date for this exact team.
Find outcomes from similar projects, then treat that pattern as the starting estimate.
Keep the team's schedule unchanged until a unique problem appears inside the project.
questions.explanation: The outside view starts with similar cases. It does not erase local context, but it anchors the forecast before the team's story adjusts it.

questions.prompt: Helena says Jack can ignore restaurant failure rates because passion and a good menu make his Thai place different. Which reply fits the source case?
choices: Passion may help Jack execute, but it does not remove his restaurant from the reference class.
Passion proves Jack's case belongs outside any base-rate comparison with other restaurants.
Passion should be the only evidence considered until Jack's first month of sales is known.
questions.explanation: Jack's inside story may matter, but it cannot cancel the restaurant category. The failure rate is the anchor his forecast has to face.

questions.prompt: Grace's curriculum team knows that similar projects take longer, yet the group still trusts its short plan. What does Kahneman's case warn about?
choices: A team should trust the short plan when it understands each task in more detail than outsiders do.
A team should treat expert status as proof that the outside view has already been applied.
A team can know the base-rate evidence and still let commitment make its own project feel special.
questions.explanation: Expertise does not cancel insider bias when the project is personal. The team can know the comparison and still discount it.

questions.prompt: When Ethan's remodel contractor offers a confident finish date, which follow-up best turns the expert's experience into a base-rate forecast?
choices: Can you promise this exact remodel will finish before school begins?
For homes like ours, how often does this kind of remodel miss its first date?
Which confident date would make our family feel least anxious this week?
questions.explanation: Experts help when they turn experience into a base rate. A precise promise about one case can sound useful while giving less evidence.

questions.prompt: Justine has survival probabilities for a bone marrow transplant but still asks patients what recovery felt like. What evidence is she adding?
choices: A replacement for the probabilities, since averages should leave once stories arrive.
A check on whether the medical team can give a more exact single prediction.
A close-up view of burdens and practical details the average does not show.
questions.explanation: Patient accounts reveal lived demands. They do not replace the statistics; they add the day-to-day texture the statistics leave out.

questions.prompt: Cyrielle hears one powerful transplant story and wants to treat it as the deciding evidence. Which correction keeps zooming in honest?
choices: Use the story as the main forecast because firsthand experience is more concrete than odds.
Drop the story from the choice because any single patient account will distort judgment.
Treat the story as lived detail that complements, but does not replace, the broader transplant evidence.
questions.explanation: Zooming in is not trusting one anecdote over data. The patient story adds texture while the broader evidence still anchors the choice.

questions.prompt: Curtis has a base rate for new restaurants and site notes from the actual block he may lease. Which reality test is complete enough?
choices: Run only the base-rate math, since reality testing means the numbers settle the choice.
Start with the comparable restaurant outcomes, then adjust for concrete site details that truly matter.
Use the block's foot traffic first, then look for base rates only if the lease feels risky.
questions.explanation: Reality includes aggregate outcomes and lived details. The better order starts with the class, then tests which local facts deserve an adjustment.

questions.prompt: Your team says its software rollout is too unusual for comparison because the plan feels cleaner than past rollouts. What should happen next?
choices: Find a useful comparison group anyway, then make only evidence-based adjustments for real differences.
Accept the team's uniqueness claim if the rollout plan has fewer visible flaws than older plans.
Wait to use base rates until the rollout has failed enough to prove it belongs to a class.
questions.explanation: Exceptional-feeling plans are exactly when base rates matter. Most plans still have a reference class, even if the first match is imperfect.

reviewCards.front: What does zooming out ask before a forecast gets trusted?
reviewCards.back: It asks what happened in similar cases. The base rate becomes the starting estimate before local detail or confidence gets to move the number.

reviewCards.front: Why can the inside view make a plan feel safer than it is?
reviewCards.back: The details feel special and vivid, so the decision maker may underweight comparable outcomes. Jack's Thai restaurant plan still belonged to the restaurant class.

reviewCards.front: How should you use an expert when you need the outside view?
reviewCards.back: Ask for reference classes and common outcomes: how often similar cases work, miss dates, or fail. A base-rate answer can beat a confident one-case prediction.

reviewCards.front: What does zooming in add that base rates may miss?
reviewCards.back: It adds lived detail: what the choice feels like, requires, and changes day to day. Brian Zikmund-Fisher's patient accounts added texture to transplant odds.

reviewCards.front: What are the four parts of the Two evidence lenses framework?
reviewCards.back: Zoom out to base rates, Ask experts for reference classes, Zoom in to lived detail, and Combine aggregate and close-up evidence.

reviewCards.front: What does Consider the opposite (Ch 5) get WRONG if you apply it naively to Zoom Out, Zoom In?
reviewCards.back: It might keep asking for contrary evidence but miss the base rate. In this case, reality testing also needs the outside view and close-up experience, not just dissent.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Two-Lens Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice moving a forecast through two distances. First name the reference class and its base rate. Then add only the close-up details that would change the estimate in a visible way.

ifThenPlans.context: If a plan starts sounding one of a kind
ifThenPlans.plan: If the case feels unique, then Run the Two-Lens Check by naming the nearest comparison group before you discuss local advantages.

ifThenPlans.context: If an expert offers one confident date or outcome
ifThenPlans.plan: If the expert gives a point prediction, then ask for the reference class and the usual range for cases like yours.

ifThenPlans.context: If a story makes the numbers feel cold
ifThenPlans.plan: If a lived account changes the room, then write what it adds to daily reality and check whether it should move the base estimate.

ifThenPlans.context: If one anecdote starts to dominate the choice
ifThenPlans.plan: If one story takes over, then mark it as texture and return to the broader pattern before changing the decision.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a forecast crosses your desk, move the forecast page beside your best comparison note. Leave it there until you write one reference class and one lived-detail adjustment.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, run a swap experiment. For the first half, judge one small choice from its inside story first. For the second half, start with the base rate, then compare which half produced the clearer call.

memorableLines.text: Base rates cool the story before the story runs the room.
memorableLines.why: It gives the outside view a simple image and a reason to use it.

memorableLines.text: Close-up stories warm the average without letting it drive alone.
memorableLines.why: It protects both data and lived detail in one line.
