chapters.title: Ooch
chapters.hook: 1 jungle trial can beat 12 forecast slides before a company bets big.
chapters.counterintuition: Ooching is not dabbling, but asking reality for a cheap answer before pride buys an expensive one. The small move matters only when it tests the guess that could change the choice.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, add one line above it: "What am I guessing?" Tally 1 if the reply predicts instead of asking for a small test.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a safe test can touch the main uncertainty, ooch first: run a small real experiment, watch behavior, then decide with evidence instead of guesses.

breakdown.fastRead:
John Hanks did not ask a slide deck to imagine a jungle. National Instruments had wireless sensors to judge, and the Costa Rican jungle could answer a question the office could only guess at. Heat, rain, distance, and rough use would speak quickly. Tiny tests make guesses face the weather.

Ooching means taking one small real step before a big commitment. It is not a toy version of every choice. It is a test aimed at the assumption that matters most. If the field trial, customer click, or work sample can teach you something real, do that before the debate grows grand.
breakdown.deepRead:
Forecasts feel neat because they keep the mess offstage. A test puts the mess back where you can learn from it. The mechanism is simple: name the guess, make it small enough to try, and measure behavior rather than approval.

Cars Direct dot com faced a plain market question: would people buy cars online? A survey could collect nice intentions. A forecast could make the market look large or small. A small sales test asked for stronger proof. Would a shopper move from interest to purchase when the car, price, and online process were real? A good ooch changes the next step.

Saras Sarasvathy found a similar habit in skilled founders. Under high uncertainty, they do not wait until the far future becomes clear. They choose affordable actions and learn from the people who respond. Scott Cook's culture at Intuit fits the same pattern. Product leaders can argue for weeks about what users might prefer. Or they can run a clean experiment and watch what users do.

This is why ooching beats debate when a small test is possible. It does not claim that every choice is easy. It only says that some guesses are testable sooner than they look. The reader's job is to find the live guess. If the test can touch it cheaply, let the world answer before the room votes.
breakdown.fullRead:
A hiring desk shows the same idea without a jungle or a startup. Dana can interview three people and leave with a strong feeling about polish. Or she can ask each finalist to complete a short work sample like the job they would do on Monday. The interview shows who performs well in an interview. The sample shows more of the work.

That distinction is the heart of ooching. A useful test reaches the claim that will decide the choice. If the claim is, this candidate can write clear customer notes, the work sample should include a customer note. If the claim is, this feature will save users time, the test should watch users try it. If the claim is, these sensors can survive a harsh field setting, the field site belongs in the test.

Phil Tetlock's forecasting work adds humility to the tool. Experts can know a lot and still miss complex futures. That does not make expertise worthless. It means confidence should not be treated as a receipt from the future. When a real test is near, the wise move is to trade some prediction for contact with the world.

The Ooch filter has four parts: Name the riskiest assumption, Design a small real test, Measure actual behavior, and Avoid ooching when commitment is required. The first part stops busywork. A test of a side issue can feel useful while leaving the main risk untouched. The online car seller did not need only comments about whether online buying sounded modern. It needed evidence that buyers would act.

The second and third parts keep the test honest. Small does not mean vague. A good test has a real setting, a real user, a real task, or a real field condition. John Hanks learned from sensors in the place they had to work. Scott Cook's product teams learn when users meet the product, not when managers admire a mockup.

The fourth part is the guardrail. A small test can hide a large dodge. Some choices need full weight before they can teach you anything. A marriage, a mission-critical hire, a safety pledge, or a team commitment may fail if treated like a sample tray. The person most misled by ooching is the leader who keeps asking for one more tiny test because a real yes would bind them.

Use the tool when the world can answer cheaply. Do not use it to postpone a choice that only becomes real through commitment. A good ooch is small, live, and aimed at the risk. When it cannot meet those three tests, stop sampling and make the call.

examples.title: Jungle Field Memo
examples.scenario: On Monday at the field-trial desk, Dana drafts a memo to the National Instruments team. It begins, "Forecasts do not sweat." She lists John Hanks, wireless sensors, and the Costa Rican jungle. Then she writes the live choice: send a small kit into rain and distance before a larger bet, or keep refining the office model.
examples.whatToDo: Dana turns the sensor forecast into a memo that names the exact field condition to test, then asks for a small jungle trial before the team scales the bet.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo keeps the case in the real use setting. The lesson travels whenever a forecast needs weather, users, or rough handling before money moves.

examples.title: Survey Versus Sale
examples.scenario: At a Friday online car sales review for Cars Direct dot com, Clemence brings an internet retail forecast built from survey interest. Reagan opens the mock sales page and pushes for a market test: show a real car, a real price, and a path to buy. Clemence gets language about what shoppers like. Reagan gets a sharper signal about whether they will act.
examples.whatToDo: Reagan keeps the forecast as background, then sets up a small Cars Direct dot com purchase test so stated interest has to meet real buying behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why demand is stronger when customers act. A market can answer a narrow question before a full plan hardens.

examples.title: Founder Reframe
examples.scenario: Stuart tells Clara on a founder coaching call that the market forecast still feels foggy. Clara answers with Saras Sarasvathy's effectuation work and Scott Cook's experiment habit at Intuit. "Do not predict the whole road when you can buy one honest mile," she says. Stuart stops polishing the forecast and names one affordable user test.
examples.whatToDo: Clara redirects Stuart from a perfect market prediction to one affordable action that can draw a real response from users or partners.
examples.whyItMatters: The talk makes the entrepreneurial move plain. Under uncertainty, control a small next action instead of pretending to know the distant market.

examples.title: Interview Work Sample
examples.scenario: Ophelie faces a whiteboard during an onboarding class and draws two boxes for a mock hiring choice. One says interview answer; the other says work sample. Irene, a new supervisor, asks why charm cannot be enough. Ophelie gives the class a real customer note task and says the sample will test Monday's work, not Friday's polish.
examples.whatToDo: Ophelie turns the lesson into a short work sample, so Irene can compare interview shine with the task the new hire would actually perform.
examples.whyItMatters: The classroom shows ooching outside product tests. When the risk is performance, a small sample of the work can beat a smooth conversation.

examples.title: Side Question Shift
examples.scenario: Mina's first Intuit experiment plan asks whether users like the color of a new prompt. The room can run it fast, but it says little. Later, after Scott Cook's test-first habit comes up, Mina rewrites the plan around the harder question: will users finish the task faster with the prompt in place? The same test slot now points at the risk.
examples.whatToDo: Mina changes the experiment from an easy preference check to a task-speed test that can decide whether the product idea is worth more work.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-later view protects the tool from theater. Small tests matter only when they touch the assumption that would change the decision.

examples.title: Commitment Check
examples.scenario: On a Thursday phone call, Irene holds the team pledge draft and says, "Let's ooch it for one more week." Dana answers, "John Hanks could test sensors because the jungle could teach him. What will a half-pledge teach us?" Irene says, "Maybe that we are still scared." Dana replies, "Then the test is the commitment."
examples.whatToDo: Dana separates a real field test from a delay tactic, then asks Irene whether the next small move would teach anything the full pledge would not.
examples.whyItMatters: The dialogue keeps ooching from becoming a fancy name for hesitation. Some choices only produce evidence after people fully enroll.

questions.prompt: A product lead can run a one-week pilot before signing a large contract. Which move best fits ooching?
choices: Run the pilot to gather real feedback on the risky assumption before the larger commitment.
Shrink the contract slightly so the final choice feels less exposed to criticism.
Debate the contract longer until the team feels more comfortable with its forecast.
questions.explanation: Ooching uses a small experiment to replace unsupported prediction with evidence. A smaller contract or longer debate may not test the key uncertainty.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing a wireless sensor plan like John Hanks's National Instruments case. What would the Costa Rican jungle add?
choices: It would make the lab forecast look more complete by adding a vivid travel story.
It would expose real field limits that an office or lab model might miss.
It would prove the sensors should launch if the team already likes the forecast.
questions.explanation: The jungle is not decoration. Rain, distance, and rough use can reveal technical and practical constraints that office speculation misses.

questions.prompt: A policy team trusts expert forecasts because the experts know the field well. Which reply fits the Tetlock lesson behind ooching?
choices: Expert knowledge removes the need for direct tests when the field is complex.
Expert forecasts should be accepted first and checked only after a public failure.
Expertise helps, yet uncertain futures still deserve direct tests when tests are available.
questions.explanation: Tetlock's work supports humility about prediction. Expertise matters, but a real test can beat confidence when the future is hard to forecast.

questions.prompt: At a Cars Direct dot com pilot review, Reagan asks whether people will buy cars online. Which evidence best tests that question?
choices: A survey asking shoppers whether online car buying sounds convenient.
A small market test that lets shoppers move toward an actual online purchase.
A forecast deck estimating internet retail growth from broad traffic trends.
questions.explanation: Cars Direct needed behavior, not only stated interest. Actual purchase steps are stronger evidence than a survey or a broad internet forecast.

questions.prompt: A founder says Saras Sarasvathy's effectuation work means entrepreneurs should predict the market more carefully. What is off in that reading?
choices: It treats stakeholder response as less useful than a polished long-range forecast.
It makes affordable action sound like a backup plan after prediction succeeds.
It misses that founders can choose affordable tests and learn without perfect prediction.
questions.explanation: Effectuation favors action under uncertainty. The founder can take an affordable step and learn from response instead of trying to see the whole market first.

questions.prompt: At an Intuit product review, two leaders argue about what users will prefer. Which move matches Scott Cook's experiment culture?
choices: Let the senior leader choose the preferred design so the team can move quickly.
Run a clean user experiment so behavior can settle the product debate.
Keep debating until both leaders can explain the same user forecast.
questions.explanation: Scott Cook's culture favors experiments that reveal user behavior. A leader's preference or a shared forecast is weaker than watching users act.

questions.prompt: When a hiring panel for a customer-support role leaves impressed by a candidate's smooth interview, which next step uses the work-sample lesson?
choices: Treat the interview as the strongest evidence because it showed poise under pressure.
Ask a few more interview questions so the panel can confirm the same impression.
Give a short job-like task so the panel can see performance instead of interview skill.
questions.explanation: A work sample tests the work more directly. Interviews can reward impression management, so more interview talk may repeat the same weak signal.

questions.prompt: Your team keeps asking for tiny tests before making a pledge that only works if everyone joins fully. What warning applies?
choices: Ooching may be avoidance when the situation needs real commitment to teach anything.
Ooching should continue until no one on the team feels any doubt about the pledge.
Ooching is safer than commitment whenever the team can define a smaller sample.
questions.explanation: Some choices cannot be sampled without weakening them. If the test dodges the commitment itself, it delays responsibility instead of producing evidence.

questions.prompt: A team proposes an easy test that will not touch the risk driving the launch decision. What should change?
choices: Aim the test at the riskiest assumption so the evidence can change the decision.
Keep the easy test because any small action gives the launch more discipline.
Pick the test that leaders can finish fastest so the launch keeps its momentum.
questions.explanation: A useful ooch targets the central uncertainty. Testing a side question can create false comfort while the real launch risk stays untouched.

reviewCards.front: What does ooching ask you to do before a large commitment?
reviewCards.back: Run a small, low-commitment experiment that tests the assumption most likely to change the decision. The point is real feedback before the big bet.

reviewCards.front: Why did the Costa Rican jungle matter in the John Hanks sensor case?
reviewCards.back: The jungle was the real use setting. Rain, distance, and rough conditions could reveal problems that a National Instruments office forecast might miss.

reviewCards.front: What did Cars Direct dot com need beyond survey interest?
reviewCards.back: It needed behavior. A market test could show whether shoppers would move toward buying cars online, not only say the idea sounded useful.

reviewCards.front: What are the four parts of the Ooch filter?
reviewCards.back: Name the riskiest assumption, Design a small real test, Measure actual behavior, and Avoid ooching when commitment is required.

reviewCards.front: When can ooching become the wrong move?
reviewCards.back: It misfires when a tiny test avoids a choice that needs full commitment. In that case, sampling can become delay rather than learning.

reviewCards.front: Recall Analogical search (Ch 4): name one concrete ooching moment where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Cars Direct dot com could borrow the solved pattern of testing demand with behavior rather than copying a forecast. The analogy helps only after the team adapts it to online car buying.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Small Reality Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a prediction into one small contact with reality. Name the riskiest assumption, choose the smallest honest test, then record what people actually do. Use the Small Reality Check only when the test can teach without hollowing out a needed commitment.

ifThenPlans.context: If a test feels easy but does not touch the launch risk
ifThenPlans.plan: If the test dodges the hard assumption, then Run the Small Reality Check by rewriting it around the one result that could change the decision.

ifThenPlans.context: If customers praise an idea but have not acted
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise is the main evidence, then create one small buying, signing, or use step and watch whether behavior follows the words.

ifThenPlans.context: If an interview leaves everyone charmed
ifThenPlans.plan: If charm is driving the hiring choice, then add a short work sample that mirrors the task the person would do on the job.

ifThenPlans.context: If another small test would only delay a pledge
ifThenPlans.plan: If the choice needs full enrollment, then stop sampling and name what commitment must be made before new evidence can appear.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before you send your next reply about a decision, count each prediction you are making. Record one as a Small Reality Check with the assumption, test, and behavior to watch.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Teach the Small Reality Check to one person this week. Use John Hanks, Cars Direct dot com, or a work sample to explain why the test must touch the riskiest assumption.

memorableLines.text: Tiny tests make guesses face the weather.
memorableLines.why: It turns ooching into a concrete image and a portable rule.

memorableLines.text: A good ooch changes the next step.
memorableLines.why: It distinguishes real evidence from busywork in eight words.

memorableLines.text: A small test can hide a large dodge.
memorableLines.why: It preserves the hard edge without dulling the tool.

chapters.title: Overcome Short-Term Emotion
chapters.hook: A pen glides toward the car-lot form, then stops above the blank signature line.
chapters.counterintuition: The feeling deserves a hearing, yet it may be the worst witness: let time and distance join the room.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel pulled toward quick relief, write LATER on the nearest margin. Ask one person, "What will still matter after this feeling fades?" Record their exact phrase.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before a hot feeling chooses for you, create distance: check time horizons, step outside the scene, and use criteria set before pressure.

breakdown.fastRead:
Andrew Hallam's best car-buying move happens before a salesperson gets close. He avoids the lot until his criteria are set: price, needs, and limits. The shiny car may still pull at him. The practiced line may still sound urgent. But the decision has a quiet ally now.

Short feelings should not get long votes. Emotional distance means giving fear, excitement, and relief less control over the next move. It does not mean ignoring feelings. It means asking what will still matter after the rush fades.
breakdown.deepRead:
A hot feeling has volume. It is close to the body, close to the face across the desk, and close to the relief of ending the discomfort. That is why distance has to be made on purpose.

Annie's choice about Karl shows the time version. The immediate moment is scary because speaking may make things awkward. The 10/10/10 method does not promise a perfect future. It asks how the choice may feel in about ten minutes, ten months, and ten years. The tool lets Annie compare the fear of the talk with the regret of silence.

Distance is a pause, not a freeze. A pause gives the calmer self a turn. A freeze refuses to choose at all. The difference matters because distance is not anti-emotion. Love, pride, fear, and loyalty carry information. Trouble starts when the newest feeling acts like the whole truth.

PayPal's Palm Pilot direction shows the work version. Familiar work can feel safer because the team has lived with it. Mere exposure means repeated contact can make an option feel better. Loss aversion means giving up current work hurts more than a similar gain feels good. Together they can make the status quo feel wise even when evidence is pointing elsewhere.
breakdown.fullRead:
A salesperson can make urgency feel like truth. A current product can make familiarity feel like proof. A hard conversation can make ten minutes of dread feel larger than ten years of regret. None of those feelings is fake. They are simply too near.

Use 10/10/10 when a choice is ruled by the next few minutes. Ask what this will feel like soon, later, and much later. The answers will not be exact. They are a way to bring the future self into a room where the present self is shouting.

Use the outsider question when the current scene is too tangled. What would a successor do with PayPal's Palm Pilot attachment? What would a best friend tell Annie if fear were not allowed to hold the pen? What would Andrew Hallam advise a buyer before the salesperson starts praising the car? The answer does not replace judgment. It gives judgment some air.

Use precommitment before pressure. Andrew Hallam's criteria matter because they are chosen away from the lot. In the lot, the buyer is tired, flattered, and ready to be done. Away from the lot, the buyer can name what a good purchase must meet. A rule made before the heat can protect a person inside the heat.

The familiar can feel true before it is tested. That is the trap in status quo bias. Mere exposure warms the current option. Loss aversion sharpens the pain of leaving it. A team can look at a weaker path and still feel that dropping it would be reckless. The feeling is real, but it is not enough evidence.

PayPal makes the business lesson easy to see because the pull is not silly. People have spent time, skill, and hope on a path. Dropping it can feel like saying the work was worthless. Emotional distance lets the team honor the effort without letting the effort choose the future.

Emotional distance comes after reality testing in the WRAP process because evidence alone may not settle the choice. A person can have data and still be caught by fear. A team can know which product works better and still hate abandoning the old one. Distance asks a different question: which feeling should have voting power after the rush passes?

The counter-case is a fire alarm, not a car lot. If smoke is under the door, 10/10/10 would be a mistake. Do not pause to admire time horizons when the right move is to leave. Distance is for choices where a temporary spike may distort judgment. It is not a license to delay action when danger is clear.

examples.title: Criteria Before Chrome
examples.scenario: Before anyone touches a door handle on the dealership lot, Shirley and Andrew Hallam divide the scarce attention. Price ceiling, mileage, safety record, and walk-away rule get written on one page. Shirley says, "If we spend our focus on chrome later, we lose the choice now." No test drive happens yet. The whole scene is the plan that keeps sales pressure from owning the frame.
examples.whatToDo: Shirley writes the car criteria before the lot can supply urgency. She makes the page the thing they obey when the pitch gets warm.
examples.whyItMatters: Pressure works best when the buyer enters empty-handed. Predetermined criteria give a person distance before charm and relief start doing the math.

examples.title: Annie's Three Horizons
examples.scenario: During a late phone call from Annie's apartment hallway, Lydia plays the steady friend while a half-written note to Karl sits on the table. Speaking feels awful, and staying quiet feels dishonest. Annie must choose: risk the awkward talk or protect the silence. Lydia asks, "Ten minutes after you tell him, what hurts? Ten months after you hide it, what hurts?"
examples.whatToDo: Lydia walks Annie through the three horizons before Annie treats today's anxiety as the full decision.
examples.whyItMatters: The tool does not erase fear. It lets a person compare a brief sting with a longer regret before choosing which pain deserves weight.

examples.title: Palm Pilot Table Talk
examples.scenario: "The Palm Pilot work is ours," Dylan says at the PayPal product table. Alexander nods toward the product pivot and asks, "Ours, or best?" Dylan answers, "Both, maybe." Alexander keeps the question narrow. "If a new team inherited this tomorrow, would they protect Palm Pilot because it works better or because dropping it hurts?" No one wins the exchange. The status quo bias becomes visible.
examples.whatToDo: Alexander asks the successor question and separates product evidence from the pain of giving up familiar PayPal work.
examples.whyItMatters: A live exchange can reveal status quo bias without shaming the team. Familiarity and loss fear are named, so evidence can speak again.

examples.title: The Lot Surprise
examples.scenario: On Saturday afternoon, Denis stands outside a dealership office as a first-time buyer. He expects Andrew Hallam's car-buying trick to be a sharper comeback. A salesperson praises the warranty, the color, and the monthly payment while Denis grips the price sheet. The reveal is plainer: Hallam's strongest move happened earlier, when he stayed away from the lot until the criteria were fixed. The win was distance.
examples.whatToDo: Denis stops admiring in-the-moment confidence and copies Hallam's earlier move: criteria first, car-lot pressure later.
examples.whyItMatters: The surprise teaches why willpower is a weak plan. Pressure loses force when the buyer arrives with a frame the salesperson did not set.

examples.title: Karl Message Thread
examples.scenario:
Riley texts Eugenie: "Annie keeps hovering over the message to Karl."
Eugenie: "Ten minutes?"
Riley: "Embarrassed. Shaky."
Eugenie: "Ten months?"
Riley: "Maybe proud she was honest."
Eugenie: "Ten years?"
Riley: "Silence sounds worse."
The thread does not choose for Annie. It shows which feeling fades and which one may stay.
examples.whatToDo: Riley turns the stuck message into three time horizons and writes the answers before urging any action.
examples.whyItMatters: A compressed exchange can slow a hot choice. The reader sees fear shrink when it is placed beside later feelings.

examples.title: Successor Reset
examples.scenario: At Monday's PayPal product review, product lead Eugenie writes Palm Pilot on the whiteboard and starts the usual defense: sunk time, known code, familiar users. Halfway through the list, she caps the marker and restarts. "Pretend a successor arrived today with no attachment to our past work. Which product pivot would that person fund?" The room names status quo bias, and old comfort loses the first vote.
examples.whatToDo: Eugenie interrupts the routine defense and asks what a successor would choose without the team's loss fear.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset protects the hard edge. Distance does not erase the team's work; it stops attachment from impersonating evidence.

questions.prompt: You are ready to accept a quick deal mainly because the pressure will end. What risk should you notice?
choices: The feeling should be ignored because emotion usually weakens any serious choice.
The feeling may be so vivid that immediate relief crowds out later consequences.
The feeling proves the decision matters and should be settled while energy is high.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 warns against temporary distortion, not emotion itself. The problem is that immediate relief can overpower later priorities.

questions.prompt: At a dealership lot, a buyer hears a persuasive pitch and feels the monthly payment getting easier to accept. Which Andrew Hallam move fits the source case?
choices: Enter the lot first, then decide which criteria feel reasonable after hearing the pitch.
Trust confident improvising because sales pressure is best handled face to face.
Set the criteria away from the lot so the salesperson has less control of the frame.
questions.explanation: Hallam's distance comes from precommitment. Criteria chosen away from the lot beat improvised confidence inside the sales moment.

questions.prompt: Annie is afraid the talk with Karl will feel awful right away, so she writes three time horizons before choosing. What is 10/10/10 meant to do?
choices: Compare how the choice may feel across near, medium, and long horizons.
Predict the exact future reaction Karl will have after the conversation.
Replace the emotional part of the choice with a cleaner logical answer.
questions.explanation: 10/10/10 creates perspective across time. It is not a precise forecast and it does not remove emotion from the choice.

questions.prompt: Lydia sees Annie treating the first wave of fear as if it settles the whole Karl choice. Which reading fits the source fact?
choices: A scary feeling now is strong evidence that the choice should wait until fear disappears.
A short-term fear can coexist with a long-term value, so both horizons need a hearing.
A future-oriented answer should cancel the present feeling before any choice is made.
questions.explanation: Annie's case does not treat fear as useless. It shows that immediate anxiety can lose power when longer regret is considered.

questions.prompt: A PayPal team keeps liking the Palm Pilot path more because it has lived with that work for so long. What bias may be active?
choices: The familiar path is probably better because repeated contact reveals hidden strengths.
The familiar path should be rejected because comfort usually means the team is lazy.
The familiar path may feel better simply because repeated contact creates comfort.
questions.explanation: Mere exposure makes repeated contact feel attractive. The comfort is not proof that the option is objectively stronger.

questions.prompt: A team overprotects old work because dropping it feels worse than a similar gain feels good. What does loss aversion explain?
choices: The old work has a larger objective value than any new option with the same upside.
The pain of giving something up can be weighted more heavily than an equal gain.
The team should avoid the loss when the matching gain looks similar on paper.
questions.explanation: Loss aversion is about psychological weight, not objective value. The pain of giving up can distort the choice.

questions.prompt: PayPal's current product direction feels safer partly because it is familiar and partly because leaving it hurts. What should the team suspect?
choices: The status quo may be winning through comfort and loss fear, not better evidence.
The status quo should win because familiar options usually carry better evidence.
The status quo should lose because any current option is mainly emotional baggage.
questions.explanation: Status quo bias can come from mere exposure plus loss aversion. The current path may feel safe without having the stronger case.

questions.prompt: Before a tense product debate, you ask what a best friend or successor would advise if they were not caught in the current feeling. What is that question for?
choices: It creates distance so your own judgment can see the cleaner priority.
It hands the decision to someone less tangled in the current feeling.
It proves personal feelings should not be included in the final choice.
questions.explanation: The outside view clarifies judgment; it does not outsource responsibility. Feelings still count, but they stop crowding the whole room.

questions.prompt: A team has reality-tested a product choice but still keeps defending the familiar path. Why does WRAP still need emotional distance?
choices: Because evidence is unnecessary once the team notices that attachment is shaping the choice.
Because emotional distance belongs before reality testing and should replace fresh evidence.
Because good evidence can still be misused when fear or attachment dominates the room.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 makes distance a separate step. Evidence helps, but people can still be captured by attachment after the evidence arrives.

reviewCards.front: What does emotional distance separate in a hot choice?
reviewCards.back: It separates a lasting preference from a short spike of fear, relief, excitement, or attachment. The feeling still matters, but it no longer gets to vote alone.

reviewCards.front: Why did Andrew Hallam's car criteria work better before the lot?
reviewCards.back: The criteria were set before sales pressure arrived. That gave the buyer a frame the salesperson did not control when the car, pitch, and relief became vivid.

reviewCards.front: What does 10/10/10 ask you to compare?
reviewCards.back: It asks how a choice may feel in about ten minutes, ten months, and ten years. The aim is perspective, not a perfect forecast of the future.

reviewCards.front: How do mere exposure and loss aversion feed status quo bias?
reviewCards.back: Mere exposure makes the current option feel comfortable. Loss aversion makes leaving it hurt. Together they can make weak evidence feel like safety.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Distance tools for creating emotional distance?
reviewCards.back: Use 10/10/10, ask the outsider question, ask the best-friend question, and precommit before pressure. Each tool gives the calmer self a turn.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more in a hot choice, analogical search (Ch 4) or emotional distance, and why?
reviewCards.back: Analogical search helps find more options. Here the options may already be visible; the danger is letting fear, familiarity, or loss pain pick among them.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Distance Mark
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making space between the hot feeling and the final choice. Run the Distance Mark by putting one cue word on a visible surface, then asking which feeling will still deserve weight later.

ifThenPlans.context: If quick relief starts driving the choice
ifThenPlans.plan: If ending the discomfort becomes the main reason to decide, then Run the Distance Mark and ask what consequence will remain after relief fades.

ifThenPlans.context: If a sales setting starts shaping the frame
ifThenPlans.plan: If the pitch feels urgent, then return to criteria written before pressure and leave if the option misses them.

ifThenPlans.context: If the next few minutes feel too loud
ifThenPlans.plan: If short fear fills the room, then write the 10/10/10 answers before treating the fear as the decision.

ifThenPlans.context: If attachment keeps defending the current path
ifThenPlans.plan: If familiar work keeps getting protected, then ask what a successor or best friend would advise with no past work to defend.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the next time you feel the pull to choose from relief, mark one visible surface with LATER. Ask one person what will still matter after the feeling fades, then write their exact words under the mark.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Across the week, use the Distance Mark three times at widening gaps. First use it on a small purchase, then on a tense message, then on a work choice with a familiar default.

memorableLines.why: It makes mere exposure and status quo bias easy to remember.

chapters.title: Honor Your Core Priorities
chapters.hook: 3 voices pull at the Interplast chart; 1 patient priority steadies the pen.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like indecision is actually a fight among real values. When every option has a claim on you, the next step is to name what must get protected.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff, place a blank note where your walk to the next task begins. Write the exact sentence you will use to protect one core priority.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Core priorities only help when they become words, rules, and removed work that protect what matters under pressure.

breakdown.fastRead:
Kim Ramire's career choice is hard even after the first rush of feeling cools. A larger role at a tech start-up sounds alive with possibility. The current job offers stability and room for work-life balance. Both sides can be honest. That is why more calm does not always produce a clean answer.

Core priorities are the long-term values and aims that should govern a hard choice. They help when attractive options collide. A real priority gets protected before pressure arrives. If balance matters, it needs a line in the decision, not a soft hope after the offer arrives.
breakdown.deepRead:
A priority works by turning a vague pull into a standard people can use. Interplast did this by naming the patient as the ultimate customer. Donors, surgeons, and leaders all mattered, but not in the same way when a tradeoff landed on the table. The patient gave the room a north star that was plain enough to repeat.

That kind of clarity matters because pressure favors whatever is loudest. A donor calls. A surgeon wants a certain schedule. A leader wants a cleaner budget. Each request can sound reasonable. Without a named priority, the last voice in the room often wins.

Wayne's Rules at Dell show the same pattern in a different form. A rule can carry judgment to people far from headquarters. It does not end thinking. It keeps the intended priority from fading when the decision moves to the field.

This is the missing half of distance. Earlier in WRAP, distance helps cool the heat of the moment. But calm does not equal a standard. Kim Ramire can step back from emotion and still face a real conflict between opportunity and balance. Interplast can care about many people and still need one answer to who comes first in a mission choice. Urgency is loud; priority is loyal.
breakdown.fullRead:
USS Benfold makes the idea physical. A Navy destroyer cannot honor a higher priority by adding one more slogan to an already full day. Captain Abrashoff and the crew had to cut time-consuming tasks. That gave attention back to work that mattered more. The calendar became part of the decision.

That is the hard edge. Declared priorities are not the same as operating priorities. The declared priority is what appears in a speech or on a wall. The operating priority is what gets protected when time, attention, money, and status compete. If a meeting always survives and the patient voice always gets squeezed, the meeting is the real priority.

Lesser priorities are not always foolish. They can be immediate, measurable, and socially rewarded. Clearing an inbox gives quick relief. Satisfying a loud stakeholder wins thanks by the end of the day. Finishing a familiar task feels safer than cutting it. Those rewards are why lesser work can crowd out the work that matters most.

Interplast shows why the words need to be plain. "The patient is the ultimate customer" is not a thick mission phrase. It is a sentence a leader can use while donors, surgeons, and office needs pull on the same case. The sentence does not make the tradeoff painless. It keeps the tradeoff from becoming a contest of volume.

So the practice has four parts. Name core priorities in words plain enough to use. Enshrine decision rules so pressure does not rewrite the promise. Protect time and attention for the priority. Discard lesser priorities when they consume the room. A slogan without subtraction is only wall art.

In personal decisions, Kim Ramire might write the real sentence before the career conversation. I will not trade all balance for a title, even if the title flatters me. In an organization, it may sound like Interplast asking which choice serves the patient first. On a ship, it may mean cutting a task the crew has always done so a higher duty gets the oxygen.

The move also needs evidence from behavior. Do not ask only what people praise. Ask what they fund, measure, protect, and stop doing. A team that names customer care but guards only internal reports has already answered. The reports may matter, but they are getting the shelter.

The danger is overcorrection. A person can turn core priorities into rigid armor and stop learning from new facts. An organization can rank one stakeholder so harshly that it misses real duties to others. A ship can cut a task that looked lesser but quietly protected safety. Honoring priorities is not permission to stop thinking. It is a way to keep the right thing in the room while thinking happens.

examples.title: Patient First Chart
examples.scenario: "The donor wants the schedule first," Brayden says, pencil hovering over the Interplast patient chart. Lyle keeps his hand on the page. "And the surgeon wants the room." Brayden nods toward the empty line for the next decision. "Who is the customer?" Lyle says, "The patient." Brayden writes that word before he writes any request.
examples.whatToDo: Brayden names the patient before listing donor or surgeon demands, then uses that word as the first test for the decision.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows how a priority can settle a crowded room. It does not erase other voices; it ranks them for this kind of mission choice.

examples.title: Offer List Correction
examples.scenario: Anna underlines the tech start-up title on Kim Ramire's career notes and starts writing as if the bigger role should decide the page. Halfway through the sentence, she sees the mistake. She has treated stability and work-life balance as small afterthoughts. Her pen returns to the left margin, where she writes, "These are real values too."
examples.whatToDo: Anna corrects the list before it becomes a verdict, giving opportunity, stability, and work-life balance explicit space on the page.
examples.whyItMatters: Some choices stay hard after emotion settles because both sides matter. The recovery keeps the decision from mistaking flattery for priority.

examples.title: Benfold Task Memo
examples.scenario: During an afternoon watch on USS Benfold, crew lead Gordon writes a memo in the task log. It begins: "Captain Abrashoff has asked what work no longer earns its place." The next line is not a slogan. It lists duties that consume crew attention without matching the ship's higher priorities. Gordon circles two items and writes, "Stop or delegate before adding another promise."
examples.whatToDo: Gordon turns the priority into a removal list, marking lower-value work before the crew accepts new demands.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo makes priority visible in time and attention. A schedule that never subtracts will keep serving the old work.

examples.title: Two Interplast Paths
examples.scenario: At an Interplast planning table before a patient case review, Colette builds the sheet by giving the donor, surgeon, patient, and office the same weight. Her page fills with arrows, and the patient line waits. Maureen starts with the patient as the ultimate customer. Donor timing and surgeon preference still appear, but they sit below the patient need. One plan spreads attention; the other gives the tradeoff a spine.
examples.whatToDo: Maureen ranks the patient first, while Colette treats every stakeholder claim as equal and watches the decision blur.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why priority is different from politeness. Some missions require a clear first customer so daily tradeoffs do not drift.

examples.title: Career Reframe Call
examples.scenario: On a phone call after Kim Ramire's offer packet arrives, Gabrielle listens from her desk while Kim names the start-up role, the current job, and the pull of work-life balance. The call has no dramatic pause; only the soft click of a pen cap. "Calm is not a compass," Gabrielle says. "Write what the choice must protect before you compare the offers again."
examples.whatToDo: Gabrielle moves the conversation from offer features to protected values, then asks Kim Ramire to write the standard first.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe keeps distance from becoming drift. When both options carry real value, the decision needs a priority line, not just less emotion.

examples.title: Priority Class Log
examples.scenario: During a morning leadership class, Adrian studies a USS Benfold schedule beside a values statement. The class has been told that priorities guide decisions, but the columns confuse him. The statement praises higher-value work; the log protects old tasks. Captain Abrashoff's case gives the instructor one question for Adrian: "Which priority got the crew's hours?"
examples.whatToDo: Adrian checks the stated priority against the schedule, then marks which tasks actually received time and attention.
examples.whyItMatters: The school case makes the invisible test simple. Behavior follows protected routines, not the sentence everyone says they believe.

questions.prompt: You are weighing two attractive paths, and one feels urgent because people are waiting for an answer. What should a core priority do here?
choices: It should follow the option that creates the quickest relief from pressure.
It should wait until the urgent demand fades enough to reveal the easier path.
It should guide the choice by a durable value, not by the pressure of the moment.
questions.explanation: Core priorities represent long-term aims. Urgency may be real, but it is not the same as the value that should govern the decision.

questions.prompt: Kim Ramire has set the start-up offer beside notes on stability and work-life balance. Her feelings have cooled, but the page still pulls both ways. What does that show?
choices: The decision may still be hard because opportunity, stability, and balance all carry real value.
The decision should now be easy because cooling emotion removes the main source of conflict.
The decision should favor the larger role because a calm mind can now trust the strongest signal.
questions.explanation: Kim Ramire's case is not just emotional noise. It is a values conflict, so calm helps but does not supply the priority by itself.

questions.prompt: An Interplast leader faces donor pressure, surgeon preference, and a patient need on the same case. Which standard fits the source example?
choices: Give each stakeholder the same weight so no group feels pushed aside.
Treat the patient as the ultimate customer when those claims conflict.
Let the strongest outside request decide when the mission language feels broad.
questions.explanation: Interplast used the patient as the ultimate customer. Other stakeholders mattered, but the patient priority gave conflicts a clear standard.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit sends teams into the field with the same mission statement, yet each team ranks daily tradeoffs differently. What is likely missing?
choices: More shared enthusiasm for the mission before any field rule is written.
Explicit priority language, rules, or examples that can guide repeated choices.
A promise that each team can interpret the mission in its own local way.
questions.explanation: Mission agreement can still leave daily choices vague. Enshrined priorities give people repeatable language or rules for pressure moments.

questions.prompt: A field employee is away from headquarters with a customer problem and no time for a long approval chain. How can a rule like Wayne's Rules help?
choices: It can encode the intended priority so judgment travels to the edge of the organization.
It can remove the need for judgment by giving every future case the same answer.
It can protect headquarters from hearing about exceptions in the field.
questions.explanation: Good rules do not kill judgment. They carry the priority to people who must act away from the room where it was named.

questions.prompt: USS Benfold already has a full schedule when a higher priority gets named. What should the crew inspect first?
choices: Which old tasks can stay untouched while the crew works harder around them.
Which lower-value tasks should be stopped, delegated, or reduced to protect attention.
Which new slogans can make the higher priority feel visible without changing routines.
questions.explanation: The USS Benfold case shows that a priority often needs subtraction. Without removing lesser work, the old load defeats the new aim.

questions.prompt: A manager says customer care is the top priority, but every protected hour goes to internal status work. What should the manager infer?
choices: The stated priority is enough as long as the team can repeat it clearly.
The status work is harmless if it feels urgent and produces visible progress.
The operating priority is the work that receives protected time and attention.
questions.explanation: Behavior follows what gets protected. If the calendar always shields status work, that work is acting as the real priority.

questions.prompt: You keep choosing quick, measurable tasks over the slower work you claim matters most. What makes those lesser priorities so tempting?
choices: They often give fast relief or approval, even when they should not govern the decision.
They are usually trivial distractions with no real use for the team or person.
They should become the core priorities once they prove easier to measure.
questions.explanation: Lesser priorities can be useful and appealing. Their quick rewards are exactly why they can crowd out slower core priorities.

questions.prompt: A team uses distance to cool the emotion around a choice, then drifts toward the convenient option. What did distance fail to supply?
choices: A calmer mood that makes the convenient option feel less tense.
A longer pause so the team can wait for pressure to fade on its own.
A positive standard that names what matters after the emotion cools.
questions.explanation: Distance cools heat, but it does not name the value to protect. Core priorities finish the job by giving the choice a standard.

reviewCards.front: When a hard choice stays hard after feelings settle, what should core priorities name?
reviewCards.back: They should name the durable values and aims that deserve protection. Kim Ramire's choice stayed hard because opportunity, stability, and balance were all real claims.

reviewCards.front: How did Interplast make stakeholder conflict easier to judge?
reviewCards.back: It named the patient as the ultimate customer. That gave donor, surgeon, and office demands a clear standard when they pulled in different directions.

reviewCards.front: Why does USS Benfold make subtraction part of honoring a priority?
reviewCards.back: Attention is finite. Captain Abrashoff's crew could protect higher priorities only by reducing tasks that consumed time without matching value.

reviewCards.front: What reveals the difference between a stated priority and an operating priority?
reviewCards.back: Look at what gets protected when time and attention compete. The operating priority is the one that survives in the calendar, routine, and tradeoff.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Priority practices for turning values into behavior?
reviewCards.back: Name core priorities, Enshrine decision rules, Protect time and attention, and Discard lesser priorities. Each practice turns a value into something people can use.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate Two evidence lenses (Ch 6) in your own words, then use it on a core-priority choice?
reviewCards.back: Two evidence lenses means checking both the broad pattern and the lived detail. For core priorities, use it to test whether the stated value matches the actual schedule and tradeoffs.

implementationPlan.title: Write the Priority Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a value into a sentence that can guide a real tradeoff. Write the Priority Line by naming what must be protected, then check whether your time, rules, or refusals protect it.

ifThenPlans.context: If a choice stays hard after the emotion cools
ifThenPlans.plan: If calm does not settle the decision, then Write the Priority Line before comparing the options again.

ifThenPlans.context: If several stakeholders make reasonable claims
ifThenPlans.plan: If every request sounds fair, then write who or what the mission serves first and judge the requests from there.

ifThenPlans.context: If a new priority lands on a full schedule
ifThenPlans.plan: If the calendar is already full, then remove or delegate one lower-value task before accepting the new priority.

ifThenPlans.context: If urgent small work keeps winning
ifThenPlans.plan: If quick tasks crowd out the slower priority, then mark the reward they offer and choose whether that reward should govern.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, before one tradeoff conversation, prewrite the exact sentence you will say: "The priority I need to protect is __, so I can/cannot __."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, keep a three-column daily log: claimed priority, protected time or rule, lesser priority that tried to crowd it out.

memorableLines.text: A real priority gets protected before pressure arrives.
memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter's main idea into a test the reader can use.

memorableLines.text: Urgency is loud; priority is loyal.
memorableLines.why: It names why short-term pressure so often beats durable values.

memorableLines.text: A slogan without subtraction is only wall art.
memorableLines.why: It makes the hard edge of behavioral priority easy to remember.

chapters.title: Bookend the Future
chapters.hook: Could the neat forecast be the trap, while the rough range keeps you ready?
chapters.counterintuition: A careful forecast can be your best estimate and still leave you exposed. The safer move is to prepare for the future that lands below or above it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next planning pass, touch your laptop lid, explain one real choice's low and high bookends to one person, and record which side you were skipping.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat the future as a range. Imagine failure, imagine wild success, then add margin before either future arrives.

breakdown.fastRead:
Byron Penstock did not need Coinstar's future to fit one tidy line. He could ask what the investment looked like if the low case arrived, then ask what opened up if the high case arrived. The range mattered more than the middle.

Bookending means placing two ends around a forecast: a lower end that hurts and an upper end that strains capacity. The future has edges. A single forecast hides both edges if the team treats it like a promise. Penstock's Coinstar analysis shows the habit in plain terms: downside risk and upside potential are part of the same choice.

A forecast is a map, not a seat belt. Once you draw the low and high bookends, planning changes. You can run a premortem to ask why the plan failed. You can run a preparade to ask what breaks if success arrives too fast. You can add safety factors, which are plain cushions for the things your estimate missed.
breakdown.deepRead:
Range thinking works because it moves worry and hope into the room before the bills come due. The lower end asks what the team would wish it had handled sooner. The upper end asks what would choke if results beat the forecast. Those questions turn forecast humility into work you can assign.

Community Solutions could not treat housing people as a smooth march from plan to finish. Legal threats and operational snarls could block the work. A premortem gives a team permission to picture that bad ending early, then name the causes while fixes are still cheap. Failure imagined early can prevent failure later.

The mirror image is not cheerleading. A preparade asks what success would demand. Softsoap makes that easier to see. If launch demand outran the pump supply, a good product could still stall in the aisle. Securing pumps before the rush protected the upside. Success can break what failure never touched.

This is why bookending belongs to WRAP's Prepare to be wrong step. Preparing to be wrong does not mean expecting defeat. It means refusing to let one forecast boss the whole plan. One end of the range protects you from shock. The other protects you from being unready for the lucky break.

Safety factors make that range visible in the plan. They are not lazy padding. They are the spare inches, dollars, permits, pumps, or staff capacity that keep small misses from becoming large failures. Margin is humility made practical.
breakdown.fullRead:
Patrice can draw a beautiful range and still fool himself if nobody is willing to act on it. A low bookend written in a memo is not the same as a legal review, a spare supplier, or a harder launch plan. Bookending starts with imagination, but it earns its keep only when the imagined future changes the work.

That precondition matters in both directions. Some teams enjoy the premortem because it sounds hard-nosed. They list ten ways the plan could die, then call the meeting mature. The hard edge of bookending is that disaster planning alone is still a narrow frame. The Softsoap case carries the other half. Rapid demand can expose the missing pump, the thin supplier, or the service desk that cannot keep up. Upside deserves preparation too.

The 100,000 Homes Campaign shows why the lower bookend is worth the discomfort. Legal and operational threats are not vague worries when a campaign has to move real people into real housing. If those threats surface late, the work slows when people most need it to hold. In a premortem, the team borrows the bad ending for a few minutes. Then it returns to the present with a better list.

Penstock's Coinstar case adds the investment version. Expected return can sound clean, but the real spread matters more than the tidy middle. A choice with a modest middle and a terrible low end is different from one with a tolerable downside and a large upside. The range tells you what kind of risk you are carrying. The average alone can blur that.

Realistic previews add one more use. When people hear only the attractive part of a role, predictable hardship arrives as betrayal. A clear preview does not try to scare them away. It lets them meet the rough parts before they commit, so later difficulty is less likely to feel like a trick. The same logic works for plans: let the rough part introduce itself early.

The future has edges. Once the team accepts that sentence, its planning gets more honest. It asks why the plan might fail, what success would strain, and where margin belongs. It also stops pretending that a careful estimate has settled the matter.

The precondition is willingness to spend attention before proof arrives. Without that, bookending becomes theater. People name the low case and keep no cushion. They praise the high case and reserve no capacity. The tool quietly assumes the team can act before the future proves which edge was real. When that assumption is absent, the meeting may sound wise, but the plan stays brittle.

examples.title: Coinstar Range Audit
examples.scenario: On Monday in the investment archive, Joan reviews Byron Penstock's Coinstar file with a pencil beside two red-circled columns: downside risk and upside potential. The expected return line had looked tidy until she finds the spread behind it. Coinstar is no longer one bet with one future. It is a range, and the lower edge now matters as much as the bright case.
examples.whatToDo: Joan marks the low and high cases beside the main forecast before she judges whether the Coinstar risk is worth taking.
examples.whyItMatters: The audit keeps one average from hiding the shape of the bet. A reader can use the same move whenever a neat number conceals the range.

examples.title: Legal Threat Premortem
examples.scenario: On the morning before the Community Solutions risk session, campaign lead Margaux stands by a note folder for the 100,000 Homes Campaign in the campaign office. If we fail, she thinks, it will not be because nobody cared. It could be a legal threat we treated as remote, or an operational step we left vague. She hates the gloom, then sees the gift in the premortem: the bad ending is still imaginary.
examples.whatToDo: Margaux writes the failure story first, then circles the legal and operational risks the team can still reduce.
examples.whyItMatters: A premortem is not gloom for sport. It lets the team use a made-up failure to prevent a real one.

examples.title: Pump Supply Before Launch
examples.scenario: At the launch supply table, Blanche has one planning page for Softsoap and three scarce lines left beside a pump sample. A defect response plan could use them all. So could the pump supply that Colgate-Palmolive might need if demand surges. Before anyone orders anything, she allocates attention to the upper bookend: success can empty shelves as surely as failure can.
examples.whatToDo: Blanche reserves planning space for pump supply and names the capacity point that would break if Softsoap demand jumps.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene makes upside practical. Planning for success means finding the bottleneck before success exposes it.

examples.title: Margin Or Speed
examples.scenario: During a Tuesday Community Solutions operations review, lead Anne studies the 100,000 Homes Campaign board with permit notes and legal threats pinned along the side. One path keeps the timeline lean and protects urgency. The other adds safety factors for permits, outreach gaps, and handoffs, but it makes the plan look slower. She weighs drag against a small miss that could stop housing work cold.
examples.whatToDo: Anne adds margin only where an estimate miss would block the work, then explains the tradeoff in plain terms.
examples.whyItMatters: Safety factors are not decoration. They belong where uncertainty can turn a small planning error into a stopped plan.

examples.title: One Forecast Conversation
examples.scenario: On the call, analyst Patrice taps a Coinstar spreadsheet beside his keyboard. "The forecast is careful," he says. Raphael answers, "Careful about which future?" The page names the middle case, but Byron Penstock's logic asks for the edges too. Patrice reads the downside risk aloud, then the upside potential. The call changes once both ends are in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Patrice keeps the forecast, then asks Raphael to test the low and high cases before the investment judgment is made.
examples.whyItMatters: WRAP's prepare-to-be-wrong move is not a vote against forecasts. It keeps a forecast from shrinking the future.

examples.title: Softsoap Upside Reveal
examples.scenario: In the product launch review, Sage lets the Softsoap slide deck begin with the expected worry: what if buyers shrug? Everyone can picture that failure. Then she flips to the next page, where demand is strong and the pump supply cannot keep up. The room had prepared for rejection. The surprise is that a hit can also break the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Sage asks for the success case first and names the pump supply as the constraint that must be ready before demand arrives.
examples.whyItMatters: A preparade catches the strain success creates. The reader learns to ask what would fail if the good news came fast.

questions.prompt: Joan sees a project plan built around one careful forecast while the team prepares the budget. Which revision best uses bookending?
choices: You should refine the central estimate until the team agrees on the most likely result.
You should delay planning until the outcome data removes the need for a range.
You should mark the lower and upper outcomes so the plan can prepare for both.
questions.explanation: Bookending treats the future as a range. A sharper middle estimate still leaves the team exposed to outcomes above or below it.

questions.prompt: A manager reads Byron Penstock's Coinstar case as a hunt for expected return alone. What is missing from that reading?
choices: The analysis treats the expected return as enough once the forecast is careful.
The analysis compares upside and downside, so the shape of the risk matters.
The analysis waits for demand data before judging whether risk is tolerable.
questions.explanation: The Coinstar case teaches asymmetry. Expected return alone can hide whether the downside is tolerable and the upside is worth it.

questions.prompt: Blanche's team is about to launch a campaign, and the risk wall is still blank before the final review. Which move fits a premortem?
choices: They should list upbeat signs so the launch meeting does not drift into worry.
They should wait for the first failure, then trace which cause mattered most.
They should imagine the campaign failed and ask what preventable causes led there.
questions.explanation: A premortem borrows a future failure while the team can still act. It is not mood management or after-the-fact review.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit director says premortems belong in corporate product work, not a housing campaign. How should Anne answer from the 100,000 Homes case?
choices: The 100,000 Homes Campaign shows that social efforts also face legal and operational threats.
The 100,000 Homes Campaign shows that legal risks matter less when the mission is urgent.
The 100,000 Homes Campaign shows that premortems are useful only after field work begins.
questions.explanation: The campaign had real legal and operational risks. Imagining failure early helped readiness outside a corporate setting.

questions.prompt: Sage expects unusually strong sign-ups for a new service and sees no staffing note in the launch plan. Which question best uses a preparade?
choices: Sage should ask which failure story would most embarrass the team after launch.
Sage should ask what supply, staffing, or service point would break if success came fast.
Sage should ask whether optimism is making the team ignore the most likely forecast.
questions.explanation: A preparade plans for the strain of success. It is not just optimism, and it is different from a failure-focused premortem.

questions.prompt: Patrice points to the Softsoap launch page and says high demand can be solved later if it happens. Which response matches the pump-supply lesson?
choices: Late capacity fixes can miss the opening, so pump supply needs attention before demand arrives.
High demand proves the launch is healthy, so supply planning should follow the sales data.
Pump supply is a downside risk, so the team should focus first on avoiding weak demand.
questions.explanation: The Softsoap case shows upside demand can be fragile. If pumps are not ready, the opportunity may pass before capacity catches up.

questions.prompt: A planner calls safety factors lazy padding while Anne marks permit delays on a campaign board. Which reply best fits bookending?
choices: Safety factors should be removed so estimates stay disciplined and lean.
Safety factors should be added only after the first miss proves the estimate was wrong.
Safety factors add margin so imperfect estimates do not turn small misses into failures.
questions.explanation: Margin answers uncertainty. It is not a reward for loose planning, and waiting for proof can make the cushion arrive too late.

questions.prompt: Margaux is hiring for hard field work and wants applicants to stay after rough days. Which preview best fits bookending?
choices: She should sell the attractive parts first and let people discover the rough parts after joining.
She should describe the predictable hardships clearly so later difficulty is not a shock.
She should keep the preview short because too much realism can weaken commitment.
questions.explanation: A realistic preview calibrates expectations. Hiding predictable hardship may create surprise and quitting later.

questions.prompt: Raphael hears Prepare to be wrong during a forecast review and assumes the team should expect failure. What correction does bookending add?
choices: Preparing to be wrong means preparing for variance, including unusually good outcomes.
Preparing to be wrong means giving the failure case more weight than the success case.
Preparing to be wrong means avoiding forecasts until the future becomes clearer.
questions.explanation: Bookending widens the imagined future in both directions. It prepares for failure and for success that strains the plan.

reviewCards.front: How does bookending change one forecast into a usable range?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to add a lower-end future and an upper-end future, then prepare for both. The middle estimate stays useful, but it stops pretending to be the whole future.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of the Future bookends framework?
reviewCards.back: The five parts are Imagine the lower bookend, Run a premortem, Imagine the upper bookend, Run a preparade, and Add safety factors.

reviewCards.front: How does a premortem turn imagined failure into useful work?
reviewCards.back: It asks the team to picture the plan failed, then name why while fixes are still possible. The value is prevention, not pessimism.

reviewCards.front: Why is a preparade different from simple optimism?
reviewCards.back: A preparade asks what must be ready if things go unusually well. It looks for supply, staffing, or service bottlenecks that success would expose.

reviewCards.front: How would WRAP (Ch 1) change the way you handle this forecast situation?
reviewCards.back: WRAP says the last move is Prepare to be wrong. For bookending, that means shaping the forecast so your plan can handle the low case and the high case.

reviewCards.front: Why can a realistic preview help people stay when the work gets hard?
reviewCards.back: It lets people meet predictable hardship before they commit. Later difficulty feels less like a trick because the rough parts were named early.

implementationPlan.title: Draw Both Bookends First
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice treating every important forecast as a range before you act on it. Draw Both Bookends First means you name the lower-end future, the upper-end future, and the margin each one needs. Then you change the plan while change is still cheap.

ifThenPlans.context: When one forecast starts to feel like the future
ifThenPlans.plan: If the middle case starts bossing the plan, then Draw Both Bookends First and write one low case and one high case beside it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a project feels too important to imagine failing
ifThenPlans.plan: If failure feels unspeakable, then Draw Both Bookends First and run a premortem on the two preventable causes you can still address.

ifThenPlans.context: When success would create its own strain
ifThenPlans.plan: If the good case would overload supply, staffing, or service, then Draw Both Bookends First and name the first bottleneck.

ifThenPlans.context: When an estimate has no cushion for ordinary misses
ifThenPlans.plan: If a small miss would stop the work, then Draw Both Bookends First and add margin at that weak point.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next day, attach this move to the first object you touch before work. When one forecast guides a choice, draw the low and high bookends on paper and record which one needs margin.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, rehearse Draw Both Bookends First on a real decision before you act. Explain the low case, high case, and safety factor to one person.
